SoloFactory 0.14 ← Back to SoloFactory

User manual

From a conversation to a running, verified app on your own machine. Your Codex or Claude subscription does the AI work; SoloFactory owns the process, the gates and the evidence.

1. Start the factory

You need Node 26 LTS or Node 24 LTS (other versions from 22 up start with a warning, in the terminal and once on this page) and a signed-in Codex or Claude Code command line, on macOS or Linux. On Windows, SoloFactory runs inside the Ubuntu (WSL2) window: run every command there and open the address in your usual Windows browser. In an installed SoloFactory folder, start it with:

bash start.sh

(From a source checkout, npm start does the same.)

Open http://127.0.0.1:4173. The status pill top right reads Factory ready when a provider is signed in. No API key is ever asked for or stored; the agents run under your subscription. If another app already uses port 4173, the factory says so and stops; start it on a free port with PORT=5000 npm start and open http://127.0.0.1:5000 instead.

Updates

The factory tells you when a newer SoloFactory is out. Open Menu at the foot of the left rail: its entry reads Update available with the new version, and opens a panel with Update now and the prompt to paste into Claude Code or Codex, with a Copy button. Update now has the open project's AI run the update, then restarts SoloFactory in the same terminal window and reloads the page; it won't start while anything is building or queued, and if it fails SoloFactory stays as it was and the panel says why (full output in update.log). Otherwise the entry reads Check for updates and shows the result beside it for a few seconds. Nothing updates until you choose to, so update when it suits you. It checks at startup, when you open or refresh the page, and when you ask; never in the background. Screenshots: the update notice.

2. Projects

A project is the folder the factory builds into. The project name at the top of the page opens a switcher; + New project there, or Menu → New project, asks for a name in a small dialog. Each project is its own git repository with the app at the root, a .aai/ folder of project context you can edit, and a run history. .aai/review.md holds your own review rules (for example "money is stored in integer cents"); every reviewer checks the app against them.

In an installed SoloFactory folder, projects live in its projects/ folder (from a source checkout, under .solofactory/projects/). A folder you create there by hand shows up too. Switching projects never interrupts a run.

The page

The left rail holds the Work list (every run of every project) and Menu. The header has the project switcher, an amber line when something needs you, the theme menu, and three tabs for the right panel: Run, Documents and Live app. The Factory Guide's conversation fills the middle. Drag the edge of the left rail or the right panel to resize it (or focus it and use the arrow keys; double-click resets it). Below 900px wide the panes stack.

3. Shape the spec with the Guide

Every app and every change starts as a conversation with the Factory Guide in the middle of the page. Tell it what you want in your own words in the box at the bottom. Enter sends; Shift+Enter adds a line. The Guide asks one thing at a time until the brief is complete, from the promise and the primary user to the acceptance scenarios and the constraints, because a vague brief is the most expensive kind of bug. Its replies are formatted text: headings, lists, bold and code.

The Guide starts with who uses the app and the moment they reach for it, before features. When there is a real choice, its one question lists two or three options and says which it would pick. Once, if a simpler app would do the job, it says so and asks. It asks what the first, empty screen shows, and raises error or phone screens only when they matter. When the question is about layout, it asks you to attach a sketch or screenshot.

As soon as the brief holds anything, the Documents panel lists it first as Draft spec, and it follows every answer. Open it to read the brief as a document. Choose Edit there to rewrite a section yourself; the edit saves into the draft at once. Ask the Guide about the document from the viewer and it runs a normal interview turn. Nothing is queued until you send it.

Already have a spec? Use Attach in the Guide box. Markdown, text, JSON, YAML and CSV files go into your turn in full; png, jpg, gif and webp mockups are saved inside the project under .factory/uploads/ and the Guide opens them. Each waiting file shows as a chip above the box (notes.md · 2k chars, mock.png · image) with an × to remove it, and you can send files without typing anything.

Profile. The Profile: … button in the Guide box picks which provider and models this project uses (see Settings). It cycles through the profiles whose provider is signed in. A run keeps the profile it was sent with.

Every run plans its features first. There is no strategy to pick. Before any code is written the factory drafts a feature plan, and an independent review has to pass it. Each feature then declares the files it creates or edits (its writes), is built, tested, reviewed and committed before the next starts, and may change only those files. Features fail smaller than one big build, and a parked run can be restarted from a chosen feature.

Checks the factory can prove. The factory can only prove what a test can run on its own. When a check needs a real folder on your computer, a real calendar date or a live outside service, the Guide rewrites it to use sample files, a test clock, a setting for the folder (such as <DocsRoot>) or a stand-in. What only a person can confirm goes in a Checked by hand after install section of the brief and in the PRD. On Windows the app runs inside Ubuntu, so a folder like D:\Docs is /mnt/d/Docs to it; that is the value to give the folder setting. A check that needs hours or days of real time or media (recordings up to 6 hours, delete after 30 days) becomes a short sample or a test clock, with the long limit kept as a setting.

4. Send to the factory

Send to the factory starts with one final review. The Guide reads the exact brief that would be frozen, your own edits included, against the interview checklist. It sizes the change first: a narrow change to an earlier run gets a one-line confirmation; a wider one gets the full check. Pressing again while that review runs does nothing, so you never pay for two.

  • Nothing missing: the brief freezes and the run joins the project's queue. The Guide shows a card saying it was sent, a run card follows its progress, and the Guide starts fresh for your next request.
  • A question: nothing is queued. The Guide asks it; answer, then send again.
  • The review adjusted the brief: nothing is queued. Read the changes in the draft spec; the next press sends it as shown, without a second review, unless you or the Guide change it first.
  • Runs in one project go one after another, each building on the tree the last one left. Queued runs move up or down within their project's queue from the Work list.
  • Runs in different projects can overlap when SOLOFACTORY_MAX_ACTIVE_RUNS is above 1.
  • A second brief for a project that already shipped becomes a follow-on release. The previous release keeps running until the new one passes its checks, then stops. If the new release fails to deploy, the previous one stays up.
  • Remove from queue drops a brief that has not started.

5. Follow a run

Click a run in the Work list, or its card in the Guide thread, to open it. The run card names the step (for example Step 3 of 7 · Build · Feature 3 of 7: Countdown) and offers Pause after this step, Cancel run, Open the spec and Open the run. The seven steps are Interview, PRD and plan, Planned features, Gates, Review, Deploy and Update docs. Build, gates and review run once for each planned feature.

Each step ends with a gate the controller owns: install, test and build (and lint, when the app declares one) must exit 0; review must pass; the deployed app must answer its health check and serve a non-empty home page. A failed gate gets at most two bounded repair attempts per feature, then the run parks. At final integration a test or proof check that fails is first rerun once, at no repair cost: if it passes, the activity list says failed, then passed when rerun, and the final review checks it as a likely race. At final integration the factory also starts the app once the way it will run live (with PORT and NODE_ENV=production), checks its health page, and stops it again. An app that crashes on start, such as one missing a production setting, fails this start check there and gets a normal repair with the start log, instead of failing later at deploy. The start check never makes the app live. If the deploy health check then fails on code that just passed the start check, the factory retries the deploy once on a fresh port before spending a repair.

  • Four or five answers sit on the Run panel. Moving? says whether work is happening and what happened last. Healthy? shows repairs used and how many acceptance cases pass. How far? counts verified features, estimates the time left, and gives the run's total time and tokens. Needs you? says No or names the one thing to do. When Resume is the step, a fifth answer, Safe to resume?, says whether the stop was a limit rather than an error (usage window, spending limit, provider outage, or your pause) and counts the features verified and new checks passed since your last Resume. If a Resume bought nothing, it says Not yet and points you to Report this run.
  • What this run did. A short summary above the controls says which features were built, how many checks passed and how many test cases they cover, and where the app is live. A paused or stopped run says nothing from it is live yet, and a rolled-back release says it is not what is live now. Waived proofs and a confirmed data backup are named. One line under it lists packages added, removed or changed and files deleted since the run started; it is information only and never holds the run. How do you know it works? opens the last result of each check, links to the end (last 64 KB) of each log, the deploy checks and each package or file change. Logs are kept only for a project's newest run, and anything a run did not record says Not recorded for this run.
  • Activity. The latest factory events, newest first, with filters for All, Agent, Files, Gates and Stages.
  • Needs you. When any project's latest run is stopped or paused, the amber line in the header names it and the browser tab reads (N) needs you. When a run is building in the project but you are looking at another one, a strip under the header says what it is doing, with View.
  • Notifications. The first time you send a run, the browser asks whether SoloFactory may show notifications. If you allow it and the hub is in a background tab, you get one notice when a run finishes (Notes is done) or stops and needs you (Notes needs you, with the reason). Your own pause sends none.

Live app and documents

The Live app panel shows whether the app is live, with Open the app and Stop the app, and aggregate metrics from the deployed app: requests, errors, average response, uptime and the busiest routes. No bodies, headers, addresses or identifiers are recorded. A stopped app offers Relaunch, which starts it again on a fresh port. When SoloFactory starts, an app that was running when it stopped (including a crash, a forced quit or a power cut) starts again on its old port (or a new one if that port is taken); an app you stopped with Stop the app stays stopped.

Each release that passes its deploy checks gets a number. The panel header shows it (Live · release 3), and the line under the address names its git tag in the app's own repository, solofactory/release/3, so you can always find or check out the exact code of a good release. Relaunching or restarting an app keeps its number; only a new release that goes live gets the next one.

Backup to GitHub. In Settings, the Backup to GitHub section backs up the open project. Press Connect: new private repo (or Use an existing repo for an empty private one) and SoloFactory uses your own gh sign-in; if you have more than one GitHub account, it asks which. It turns GitHub Actions off on that repo, so nothing ever runs there. Backup stays off until you tick Back up after each release; that first push sends every release so far. After that, each good release pushes the app's code and its release tags, and the Live app panel shows Backed up to GitHub · release 4 · 2m ago. If a backup fails, the release still counts: the panel shows the reason in amber with Retry, and the next release catches up. Your app's data (the data/ folder) is not in git, so this does not back it up. Disconnect stops backups and never deletes anything on GitHub.

The newest shipped update of a project offers Roll back to the previous release. Confirm it and the app's code goes back to the previous release, which starts again; the update's code is kept under a git tag, and data/ is never touched. The update keeps its own release tag too, and the next release gets the next number. If the update changed how the app stores its data, the panel says so and tells you to press Stop, restore the copy of data/ you backed up, then press Relaunch. Rollback is offered only when nothing in the project is running or queued.

If the app stops on its own within two minutes of starting, the panel says so in an amber line: The app stopped on its own N s after it started, so this release may be broken. On an update it names the previous release you can roll back to; press Relaunch to try again, or roll back. Nothing rolls back without you.

The Documents panel lists one brief per run, plus the draft spec while you are shaping one. Open a brief to read it.

6. The Work list

The Work list in the left rail groups every run of every project as Needs you (failed, interrupted or paused), Running, Queued and Done (shipped or cancelled), and refreshes every few seconds. An update to an app that already holds data, whose features change how it stores that data, shows Needs you · back up data/ while it builds: copy your app's data/ folder somewhere safe, tick I have backed up my app's data on the run card and press Confirm. The build carries on meanwhile; only the deploy waits, and confirming deploys it with no extra AI work. A rolled-back update leaves Done, and the previous release shows there again. Click a run to open it; if it belongs to another project the factory switches to it first. Queued runs move up or down within their project's queue, and a queued run can be removed from the queue.

7. Pause, resume, cancel, restart

ControlWhen it showsWhat it does
Pause after this stepWhile a run is buildingLets the run finish the step it is in, commits the green tree, and parks before the next one. No new agent turn starts once you press it: a failed check, a blocked review or a blocked plan parks before its repair or correction, and Resume picks that up without re-running the review. Nothing is lost and nothing is replayed on resume.
ResumeOn a paused, failed or interrupted run, when the Recovery box allows itContinues the same run, same files, from the step it stopped at. Goes to the front of the project's queue. It does not renew a spent repair budget; when the budget is spent the Recovery box offers Prepare repair plan instead. After an update, a check that failed on the older SoloFactory reruns on the new version first, at no model cost.
Cancel runWhile activeStops work now. The workspace stays as it was.
Restart from hereOn a paused, parked or cancelled run, for every finished feature after the first in the Run panel's feature listRewinds the tree to the commit before that feature and rebuilds it and everything after, exactly once. Earlier features keep their commits.
Revise the spec (Revise and resubmit on a cancelled run)On a paused, parked, cancelled or shipped runReopens the run's brief as a draft of the next revision. Tell the Guide what to change, or edit sections yourself. Resubmit to the factory runs the final review and queues the revised brief as a new run; Discard changes drops the draft. A stopped run's files roll back and it leaves the Work list, so the revision replaces it; a shipped run stays in Done and the revision builds on the live app. While a run is building its spec is read only: pause it first.
Start over from scratchOn a parked or cancelled runCreates a brand-new run from the same brief and sets the old one aside. Use it when the first feature itself is wrong.
DismissOn a parked runSets this run aside and releases the project's queue. If the app shipped before, it goes back to that release; its saved records are kept.

8. When a run parks

A run parks when a gate fails past its repair budget, a check’s test runner crashes after every test passed (no repair is spent on that), an agent hits a usage limit, sign-in, network or toolchain problem, the factory restarts mid-run, or you pause or cancel it. Known blockers are never blindly retried; a parked run holds its project's queue so nothing builds on a half-repaired tree.

When the next step needs you, a Recovery box opens under the run card. It says what happened and what the run has spent (workers, tokens, cost and time), then offers only the actions that make sense now: Resume, waive a proof you believe is wrong (with a reason in the note box), prepare or retry a repair plan (the note goes to the planner as guidance), approve a ready plan, upload a corrected plan, revise the inputs, or add a spec or prototype file. Copy recovery packet in the run's menu puts a full handoff on your clipboard for pasting into Codex or Claude when you want to fix things by hand. In the Guide thread, Let the Guide plan a repair does the same as preparing a repair plan.

The box title says in plain words why the run stopped, for example The app never answered its health check, The app stopped right after it started, The start check failed or The test runner crashed. When the factory's watchdog saw something specific, a gray What I saw line under the summary says it.

A feature that keeps failing

  • Set aside. When a feature runs out of repairs, the factory saves its work aside and keeps building every later feature that does not depend on it. Features that do depend on it wait, and the activity list says so. At the end the run parks once, with the set-aside feature's own files restored and its unspent repairs given back.
  • Repair plan. When Resume would only repeat the failure (repairs spent, the same failure on unchanged code, a feature that never reached a stable review, or specs changed), the Recovery box offers Prepare repair plan. The factory plans the unfinished work as repair features from the review findings and every spec and prototype input; each one lists the checks it closes, what it depends on and the files it writes. An independent review has to pass the plan, and then repairs start on their own.
  • A plan that stays blocked. If the plan is still blocked after its automatic corrections, the Recovery box lists the blockers and offers Download plan help packet and Choose corrected plan (a .json file), which Review this plan submits for one review. If the specs themselves are wrong, revise the inputs and prepare a new plan.
  • Repair budget. Each feature gets two repair attempts and the final full review gets two more; spent attempts are never refilled by Resume, Retry or a restart.
  • Spending ceilings. A run that has started 150 workers parks as Run worker ceiling reached; one that Claude reports has cost about $30 parks as Run cost ceiling reached (on a subscription that is list price, not a bill: it tracks how fast the run uses your weekly limit); one whose agents reported about 40M tokens parks as Run token ceiling reached, which also holds on Codex. Nothing is lost; review the spend and Resume to grant another allotment. SOLOFACTORY_MAX_RUN_WORKERS, SOLOFACTORY_MAX_RUN_COST_USD and SOLOFACTORY_MAX_RUN_TOKENS change the ceilings.

Release QA

After the last feature, the final review looks at what no single feature review could see: how features work together, whether the app is ready to deploy, and security (input checks, file paths, committed secrets, unsafe login defaults). That reviewer reports defects and does not fix feature code. For each defect it writes a failing test under qa/, and the factory hands the defect to the feature that owns the broken files for repair. At final integration the whole test suite runs, every built feature's proofs rerun, and so does every qa/ test, including those from earlier releases, so a fixed bug stays fixed.

When a prompt is too big

No prompt sent to an agent may exceed 200,000 characters; large inputs go into files the agent reads. If one ever does, the run parks with over SoloFactory's 200000-character prompt limit and no agent starts. This is a factory defect, not something your brief caused, so the Recovery box offers no Resume or Retry until a different SoloFactory build is running. Use Report this run and install the fix.

9. Report a problem

Menu → Feedback opens an Improvement form; Report this run on a stuck, paused or cancelled run opens a Problem form for that run, which can attach the run's diagnostics, scrubbed of paths and secrets. Either form switches between Problem and Improvement. Choose Preview report, then Copy report or Copy & open email: it copies the report and opens a message to support@coachlou.com with the subject "SoloFactory Feedback"; paste the report into the body and send. The body always travels through your clipboard, so you see exactly what is sent, and the hub sends nothing itself. Esc closes the form.

10. Settings

Profiles and models

Menu → Settings shows Profiles and models. A profile names a provider and, for each tier (Guide, planning and review, coding), a model and an effort. Claude and Codex are built in: Claude uses Opus medium for the Guide (with the advisor on), Opus low for planning and review and Sonnet medium for coding; Codex uses gpt-6.1-sol medium, gpt-6.1-sol low and gpt-6.1-terra low. Change a row and SoloFactory asks whether to save it as a new profile or into one of your own; a built-in profile is never overwritten. New, Save and Delete sit above the rows. Your profiles are saved to profiles.json in the factory home; a project whose profile you delete falls back to Claude. The profile Settings shows is the one the open project uses; picking another there sets it for this project and for new projects, while the Profile: … button in the Guide box switches it for one project. The other Settings rows are information for now: each shows its built-in default as plain text and names the variable that changes it. The variables below still apply and win over a profile.

VariableMeaning
SOLOFACTORY_HOMEWhere runs, projects and the demo live. Default .solofactory/ inside the SoloFactory folder (installed folders use .aai/memory/solofactory/).
SOLOFACTORY_ROOTWhere projects are discovered. Default: the home.
SOLOFACTORY_MAX_ACTIVE_RUNSHow many projects may build at once. Default 1.
SOLOFACTORY_MAX_RUN_WORKERSWorkers one run may start before it parks for your go-ahead (Resume grants another allotment). Default 150; 0 turns the ceiling off.
SOLOFACTORY_MAX_RUN_COST_USDDollars of Claude-reported cost one run may spend before it parks for your go-ahead (Resume grants another allotment). Default 30; 0 turns the ceiling off. Codex reports no cost, so a Codex run is held by the token and worker ceilings.
SOLOFACTORY_MAX_RUN_TOKENSTokens (input, cached included, plus output) one run may use before it parks for your go-ahead (Resume grants another allotment). Default 40,000,000; 0 turns the ceiling off. Both Claude and Codex report tokens, so this ceiling holds on Codex too.
SOLOFACTORY_RESTART_APPSSet to 0 to stop SoloFactory starting your apps again when it starts. Default on: an app that was running when SoloFactory stopped starts again, on its old port when that port is free.
SOLOFACTORY_UPDATE_CHECKSet to 0 to turn off the check for a newer SoloFactory release. Default on.
SOLOFACTORY_CLAUDE_MODELClaude model for builders and repairs. Default sonnet.
SOLOFACTORY_CLAUDE_EFFORTClaude effort for builders and repairs. Default medium.
SOLOFACTORY_CLAUDE_REASONING_MODELClaude model for planning, plan review, correction and reviews. Default opus.
SOLOFACTORY_CLAUDE_REASONING_EFFORTClaude effort for planning, plan review, correction and reviews. Default low.
SOLOFACTORY_CLAUDE_GUIDE_MODELClaude model for the Guide interview. Default opus.
SOLOFACTORY_CLAUDE_GUIDE_EFFORTClaude effort for the Guide interview. Default medium.
SOLOFACTORY_CLAUDE_GUIDE_ADVISORAdvisor model the Guide can consult. Default opus; set it empty to turn the advisor off.
SOLOFACTORY_CODEX_MODELCodex model for every tier, over the Codex profile's own models (gpt-6.1-sol for the Guide, planning and review, gpt-6.1-terra for coding).
SOLOFACTORY_CODEX_REASONING_EFFORTCodex reasoning effort for every tier, over the Codex profile's own efforts (medium for the Guide, low otherwise).
SOLOFACTORY_AGENT_IDLE_MINUTESAgent idle deadline, reset by any output. Default 6.
SOLOFACTORY_AGENT_HARD_MINUTESAgent total safety cap. Default 45.
SOLOFACTORY_AGENT_BACKOFF_SECONDSWait before the one automatic Codex resume. Default 15.
SOLOFACTORY_PROGRESS_MINUTESShow "Progress needs checking" when a busy worker lands no gate, commit or approved plan for this long. A warning only; nothing is stopped. Default 20, 0–240, 0 turns it off.
SOLOFACTORY_LOOP_THRESHOLDStop repairing after this many identical failures on unchanged code. Default 3, 2–10.
SOLOFACTORY_SYMPTOM_THRESHOLDStop repairing after this many identical failures even though repairs changed the code (line numbers ignored). Default 4, 0–20, 0 turns it off.
SOLOFACTORY_AGENT_MAX_TURNSTool steps one Claude turn may take before it stops with agent_turn_cap. Default 150, 0–1000, 0 turns it off.
SOLOFACTORY_GATE_MINUTESHard limit for each test or proof gate; install always gets at least 10. A gate that runs out parks the run without a repair turn. Default 5, 1–60.
SOLOFACTORY_DEMO=1Run with the deterministic fixture provider instead of a real agent.
SOLOFACTORY_ISSUES_URLWhere feedback reports are filed.

11. Work from Claude Code or Codex

You don't have to use the browser. Open Claude Code or Codex in your SoloFactory folder and say "hey solofactory". The agent checks where your apps stand, tells you in a sentence, and ends every reply with numbered options. Answer with a number or in your own words.

You:   hey solofactory

Agent: Your habit tracker is live at http://127.0.0.1:49762.
       Nothing is building right now.

       1. Add or change features in the habit tracker
       2. Start a new app
       3. Open the habit tracker
       4. Report a problem with the factory

You:   1 — I want reminders, a streak counter, and dark mode

Agent: Got it, three changes. A few quick questions...
       Here's the plan: ... This uses your subscription.

       1. Go, build it
       2. Change something first

You:   1

Agent: Queued. ... Reminders are built and passed their checks (1 of 3).
       ... Done. All three work: http://127.0.0.1:49762

The options change with where you are, and Report a problem with the factory is always the last one:

Where you areWhat you're offered
No apps yetStart my first app · How does this work?
An app is liveAdd or change features · Start a new app · Open it
A build is runningHow far along is it? · Show me the plan · Pause it · Stop it
A build stopped with a problemWhat went wrong? · Pick up where it stopped · Go back to an earlier feature · Set it aside
More than one appWhich app? · Start a new app
  • Ask for several features at once. They go in as one request. The factory builds them one at a time and checks each before starting the next, so nothing reaches you untested.
  • Nothing costs you without a yes. The agent shows the plan and builds only after you say go. It also asks before pausing, stopping, or fixing a run.
  • Only real options. If you ask for something the factory can't do, the agent says so and shows your options again.
  • Reporting a problem. The agent asks what happened, drafts the same scrubbed report as the Feedback button, and tells you to email it to support@coachlou.com with the subject "SoloFactory Feedback". It never sends anything itself.

A build started from the chat also shows up in the Work list, and you can switch between the chat and the browser at any time.

Folder set up before version 0.9.1? Its instructions still point the agent at the browser, so the first time say "hey solofactory — work from the chat, following SoloFactory's drive.md."

Screenshots were taken from the demo mode (fixture provider), which is why every project is called Pocket Pulse.
